ab_painted_wall_far_right.blurb: The far-right end of the Painted Wall is the busiest sector at Moose Mountain, a string of limestone sport crags in the Kananaskis foothills reached by a long gravel-road approach. Nearly every line here is a bolted single pitch, and the bulk of them fall around 5.11, with a good handful of 5.10s and a few 5.12s above that. Kentucky Bourbon (5.12a) is the one to note. Rock quality at Moose Mountain varies a lot, even within a single climb, so check holds before trusting them. The crags are most popular in spring and fall, and the long walk-in keeps crowds modest.
ab_painted_wall_far_right.parking_note: Leave the car at the Ing's Mine trailhead off the Canyon Creek access road. The gravel road toward the crags is long and flat enough that most climbers ride a bike in, which also makes the return trip quick.

_expect.name: West Ridge - part C - Pony Express to Long John

co_west_ridge_part_c_pony_express_to_lon.blurb: This is the middle stretch of the West Ridge, the long, low cliff band across the creek from Redgarden Wall in Eldorado Canyon. The sandstone faces southwest and the climbing is almost entirely traditional, from short face and crack routes to multi-pitch outings that finish with a rappel. Grades spread from 5.7 to 5.13, with 5.9 through 5.11 the most common. Classics here include Handcracker Direct (5.10a), Pony Express (5.11c), Practice Wall (5.11a) and Mail Ridge Tower Link-Up (5.10c). The ridge is spread out, so it is often quieter than the big walls. Bring a helmet; some loose rock remains in places.
co_west_ridge_part_c_pony_express_to_lon.parking_note: Two usual choices. Park near Milton Boulder and cross South Boulder Creek on foot, or park at the east end of the canyon, cross the bridge and follow the creekside trail. Either way you end up on the trail running along the base of the ridge.
co_west_ridge_part_c_pony_express_to_lon.approach: From the creek crossing or the creekside ramp, pick up the trail that follows the foot of the ridge and walk along it to the section you want. The creek is crossed by wading or hopping rocks when it is low, and the ramp on the other route is slippery third-class.

co_redgarden_below_lower_ramp.blurb: The routes in this section start on the lower part of Redgarden Wall, the largest and tallest cliff in Eldorado Canyon, beneath the sloping Lower Ramp that cuts across the face. Nearly all of it is traditional climbing on steep faces, cracks and corners, with fixed gear of mixed age, so solid placements and calm route-finding matter. The grades run wide, from 5.6 to 5.13 with most routes in the 5.8 to 5.11 range. Suparete (5.11b) is the classic. Plan your way down before you leave the ground, since descents here can be long, exposed and slippery when wet.
co_redgarden_below_lower_ramp.parking_note: Use the parking at the east end of the canyon, then walk to the bridge and cross it. The trail from there climbs toward the base of the wall.

ky_ash_branch.blurb: Ash Branch is a young sport crag on private land just south of Muir Valley, open to visitors. Most climbs are bolted with glued hardware and lower-offs, with a few trad lines and top-rope options mixed in. Grades run from easy to quite hard, with the bulk between about 5.9 and 5.12 and a sprinkle of harder lines above. The wall catches morning sun and then goes to shade, so it tends to feel cooler than its famous neighbor. Because many routes are recent, expect some sand, loose flakes and lichen, and wear a helmet. Stay out of any line tagged as still being cleaned or finished.
ky_ash_branch.parking_note: Turn onto Fincastle Road and watch for a gravel drive on the right, about a fifth of a mile in, marked by a wooden sign. It drops steeply to a small lot. Use the marked spaces only, and do not leave a car along the drive.

nv_blue_diamond_cave.blurb: A limestone wall of up to about 200 feet sits above Highway 160 on the left end of a long cliff band near the town of Blue Diamond. Every route is bolted sport. The steepest, hardest lines (many 5.12s and 5.13s) go through and around the cave, while the left side has more vertical face climbing around 5.10. The wall faces southeast, so it is a cool-season choice, and it makes a decent fallback when other Red Rock crags are damp. The natural rock is loose, so rockfall is a real concern: wear a helmet and have your belayer do the same.
nv_blue_diamond_cave.parking_note: Drive west on Highway 160 and pull onto the right shoulder about 1.9 miles beyond the Highway 159 junction, directly opposite the wall. Park well off the pavement.
nv_blue_diamond_cave.approach: Step through the fence along the road, follow the narrow path through the wash, then climb switchbacks up the slope to the base of the overhanging face.

nc_shortoff_mountain.blurb: Shortoff anchors the southern end of Linville Gorge, with quartzite cliffs broken by horizontal bands and cracks. Climbing is overwhelmingly traditional, so you place all your own gear and build your own anchors; this is not a bolt-clipping venue. Grades spread from 5.5 to 5.12, with the middle of the range, 5.9 to 5.11, most common. The walls get good afternoon sun, and spring and fall are the favored seasons. The approach is long and strenuous, with steep switchbacks, a gully descent to the base, and brush on the final stretch. Expect a committing, quiet day rather than a quick cragging session.
nc_shortoff_mountain.parking_note: The drive ends at the dead end of Wolf Pit Road, a dirt road passing through private land. The small turnaround fills early on pleasant weekends, so arrive early and be considerate of neighbors.

nc_big_green.blurb: Big Green is a big hillside of slab, face and water-groove climbing in Panthertown Valley, in Nantahala National Forest. Nearly all the routes are traditional, mostly between 5.9 and 5.11, with a few easier ones. Friction is good, but protection is sparse and almost every climb carries a serious-fall rating, so even the easier lines deserve respect. The valley has no facilities, and trails are lightly marked, so carry a map. Spring and fall are comfortable seasons; summer is hot and parking fills on weekends.
nc_big_green.parking_note: Most climbers use the Salt Rock Gap lot on the west side, reached by gravel Forest Service roads. High clearance helps after rain, and the lot fills quickly on weekends.
nc_big_green.approach: From the lot, walk the old roadbed past the Salt Rock overlook, then take the Deep Gap trail to a pine grove. A faint path leads to a creek crossing near the falls. Cross Panthertown Creek, follow the Great Wall trail past the Boy Scout shelter, and the face appears on your left.

wa_carnival_crag.blurb: Carnival is a compact corner of Icicle Canyon just above the Eight Mile campground. It holds a small granite crag of trad lines, with a few bolted routes and a top-rope setup, alongside a cluster of steep boulders that get plenty of sun. Roped routes run from about 5.7 to 5.12, while the problems are mostly V0 to V5 with a handful of far harder ones. Boulders are generally 10 to 20 feet tall, so bring pads and a spotter. The granite has good friction and crisp edges. The approach to the boulders is short but steep.
wa_carnival_crag.parking_note: Park at the roadside pullout next to the rock outcrop at Eight Mile, about 7.4 miles up Icicle Road from town.
wa_carnival_crag.approach: From the pullout, scramble straight uphill for roughly 100 meters to reach the boulders; the crag lies nearby.

wa_clamshell_cave.blurb: Clamshell Cave is a boulder-heavy stop along Icicle Road in Leavenworth's granite canyon. The main attraction is the cave itself, where problems tackle a roof and lip with hand-crack technique, along with other short technical lines around the neighboring blocks. Most problems fall between V1 and V4, with a few harder ones, and a few roped routes ranging from about 5.7 to 5.11 are scattered nearby. Crack skills help here more than raw power. Bring pads and a spotter, since several problems are tall for boulders.

wy_killer_cave.blurb: Killer Cave is a steep amphitheater of dolomite in Sinks Canyon, a short drive from Lander. Everything is bolted sport, single pitch and pumpy, with most lines between 5.11 and 5.13 and a few above that. The hardest, most overhanging routes are in the middle of the cave, while the walls on either side are closer to vertical and give more approachable classics. Most lines stay in shade through the day, which helps in summer. The trail up is short and steep; watch for rattlesnakes near boulders and on the path.
wy_killer_cave.approach: Take the steep trail heading up to the right, which delivers you at the base of the cave. It is short but rocky, so wear sturdy shoes.
